Classifying Columns with a Decision Tree

Source: vignettes/classifier-decision-tree.Rmd
classifier-decision-tree.Rmd

From features to a classifier

fx_extract_features() turns a column of values into 477 numeric features — a value profile describing the column’s cardinality, character makeup, numeric range, token vocabulary, and lexicon hits (see vignette("feature-engineering")). Those features are the substrate the guess_data_type() router is built on. This vignette uses them for a different, more pedagogical purpose: training an off-the-shelf classifier to predict a column’s type, one row per column.

The data frame is built by data-raw/build_feature_dataset.R: one row per sample column drawn from the Sherlock, GitTables, and formex-native corpora, with the 477 features and six ontology label columns (data_type, semantic_family, semantic_type, and the format axes). We start small, then scale up to show where a single tree breaks down.

Two preliminaries matter for any model fit on these features:

  • NA means “not applicable”. A numeric statistic is undefined on a text column; letter frequencies are undefined on an all-digit column. Impute by the reason a value is missing (data-raw/make_imputation_spec.R writes a per-feature rule: zero for absence features, median + an “is-numeric” indicator for the numeric block, drop for the header features that are empty here).
  • No label leakage. Features are extracted with col_name = NULL, so the column header never enters the model. The target comes from a ground-truth crosswalk, not from guess_data_type().

The simple version: twelve types

Start with a clean, balanced problem: twelve types, 45 columns each. Ten are rigid formats (email, ein, ipv4, iso_date, hex_color, guid, isbn, zip_code, phone, currency_code); the last two, artist and director, are both columns of human names.

library(rpart)
sub  <- readRDS("data-raw/type_features_teaching.rds")   # 540 rows x 12 types
# apply the per-feature NA rules from type_features_imputation.csv
# (zero / numeric-median / drop) -- see data-raw/tree_demo.R for the helper
X    <- impute_by_spec(sub)
y    <- factor(sub$source_label)

tr   <- sample(nrow(sub), 0.7 * nrow(sub))
fit  <- rpart(y ~ ., data = cbind(y = y, X)[tr, ], method = "class")
pred <- predict(fit, X[-tr, ], type = "class")
mean(pred == y[-tr])        # ~0.96
table(truth = y[-tr], pred)

The tree reaches 0.96 test accuracy, but the two groups of types behave very differently:

Type Recall Why
email, ein, guid, isbn, iso_date, phone, zip_code, currency_code 1.00 A single feature is nearly an indicator: rx_email, rx_ein, has_at, chk_ein_prefix_rate. One axis-aligned split isolates the class.
ipv4, hex_color 0.92–1.00 Still format-driven, occasional overlap with other digit/hex codes.
artist 0.86 Human names.
director 0.67 Human names — conflated with artist.

Rigid formats are what a decision tree does best: the regex, punct, and lexicon blocks give it near-binary features, and a shallow tree carves each type out with one or two splits. But artist and director are both just people’s names. No feature distinguishes “names that are artists” from “names that are directors”, so the tree sends director columns into the artist leaf two-thirds of the time. That conflation is not a modelling bug — it is the honest statement that the values carry “person name” but not the role.

Scaling up: the full semantic ontology

Now use the whole dataset and the full semantic_type label set — 40 classes, from person and geographic down to min_max and classification_code.

d <- readRDS("data-raw/type_features_dataset.rds")   # ~6,390 columns
y <- factor(d$semantic_type)                         # 40 classes
# same impute -> train/test split -> rpart as above
Model Accuracy Macro-recall Notes
Majority-class baseline 0.247 — always predict unordered
Single decision tree 0.630 0.346 59 leaves, 40 classes

Overall accuracy (0.63) is 2.5x the baseline and sounds respectable, but macro-recall — the unweighted average of per-class recall — is only 0.35. The gap between the two numbers is the whole story. A single tree scales poorly to a broad ontology for three linked reasons:

  1. A fixed split budget, shared across all classes. One greedy tree grew 59 leaves for 40 classes. Each split it spends separating person from organization is a split it cannot spend on usd or min_max. Common classes win the competition for splits; rare ones are left in mixed leaves.
  2. Severe class imbalance. unordered (generic categoricals) is a quarter of the rows; the tree maximizes overall impurity reduction, so it is rewarded for serving the majority and ignoring the tail.
  3. A long tail that cannot be learned at all. Eight of the 40 semantic types had zero rows in the test split, and several more had one or two. Fine types that appear once in the corpus (email, url, hash at the semantic-type level) give a tree nothing to split on.

The per-class picture: format-bearing types stay strong (timestamp 0.88, administrative 0.82, year 0.74, day_of_week 0.71), while meaning-bearing types collapse (organization 0.49, usd 0.24, classification_code 0.12, min_max 0.00).

One tree, or forty models?

Is it better to train 40 binary one-vs-rest models (e.g. logistic regression), each asking “is this column type k or not?”, than one tree predicting all 40 at once? We fit both on the same split (data-raw/model_feature_demo.R has the one-vs-rest machinery; each binary model uses its class’s top discriminating features as light regularization).

Model Accuracy Macro-recall
Single decision tree 0.630 0.346
40 one-vs-rest logistic models 0.608 0.414

Macro-recall by how much training data each class has:

Class support # classes Tree recall One-vs-rest recall
rare (1–9) 12 0.00 0.17
mid (10–49) 11 0.48 0.59
common (50+) 9 0.64 0.53

So the honest answer is “it depends on the objective.” For raw accuracy the two are about tied, and the single tree is marginally ahead — because accuracy is dominated by the common classes, and the tree carves those with a few sharp splits (and can exploit feature interactions a linear model misses). For balanced performance across all 40 types, the one-vs-rest ensemble is clearly better: it lifts the rare and mid-frequency classes the single tree abandons.

Why the ensemble helps where it matters:

  • Dedicated capacity. Each class gets its own model and the full 477-feature space to draw one boundary, instead of competing with 39 other classes for a share of one tree’s splits. A rare class is no longer starved.
  • Boundaries that fit the features. Many types are linearly separable in this space because the regex and lexicon features are near-indicators; a logistic boundary captures that directly, and degrades gracefully where a tree would need a deep, data-hungry subtree.
  • Per-class thresholds. A one-vs-rest score can be thresholded per class, so a rare type is not forced to clear the same bar as the majority.

Why the single tree is still competitive (and sometimes preferable):

  • It wins on the common classes and on overall accuracy, exploiting interactions and carving the majority cheaply.
  • It is one interpretable model, handles NA natively through surrogate splits, and needs no per-model regularization.
  • The ensemble’s 40 scores are not calibrated against each other; taking an argmax across independently-fit models is a heuristic, and overlapping types (the artist/director problem, now at scale) still collide.

Practical guidance

  • A single tree is a teaching baseline, not a production classifier. A random forest or gradient boosting — many trees, each on a feature/row subsample — removes most of the single-tree starvation and would raise both numbers substantially.
  • For a broad, imbalanced ontology, prefer either an ensemble of trees or a bank of one-vs-rest models, and report macro-recall, not just accuracy, so the long tail is visible.
  • A natural design is a cascade: a cheap model for the 7-way data_type, then a per-family specialist for the fine semantic_type. This is, in spirit, what guess_data_type() already does — a router narrows the candidates, then a per-type verifier confirms — which is why it outperforms any single flat classifier on the long tail.
# Reproduce everything in this vignette:
#   source("data-raw/build_feature_dataset.R")   # build the feature matrix
#   source("data-raw/make_imputation_spec.R")    # the NA-imputation rules
#   source("data-raw/tree_demo.R")               # the two decision-tree fits
#   source("data-raw/model_feature_demo.R")      # one-vs-rest feature models
#   source("data-raw/tree_vs_ovr.R")             # tree vs 40 one-vs-rest models
